narrative:
The model predicted that you have a 61.7% chance of failing the bar exam on your first attempt. Because this probability is above the acceptance threshold, your law school application was denied.

The decision was driven primarily by three aspects of your academic record. Your class ranking at the end of your third year was the strongest factor pushing the prediction toward failure. Standing in the bottom decile, far below the average of roughly the sixth decile among accepted students, signaled to the model that you may struggle with the demands of the bar exam. Your first-year ranking in the lowest decile (compared with an average around the sixth decile for accepted applicants) added further weight in the same direction. These two performance measures outweighed everything else in the model’s assessment.

Your undergraduate GPA of 3.00, while respectable, was the third most important factor. Because it sits slightly below the 3.23 average of accepted students, it gently pulled the prediction back toward success, yet not enough to overcome the stronger negative signals from your class rankings.

Your LSAT score of 33, family income in the lower-middle bracket, full-time study plans, gender, and race played only minor roles; the model focused overwhelmingly on your school performance trends.

To improve your chances, you should consider retaking key courses to raise your class standing, investing time in a structured bar-prep program, or strengthening other parts of your profile before reapplying. Many students in similar situations have succeeded on a second attempt after targeted improvement.
